text: You get a sorted array of integers and a target value. Return the index of the target. If it's not there, return negative one. It has to run in log n time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the array is sorted in ascending order, and I need one index back, not a count. Is that right?
Are the values unique, or can the same number show up more than once?
Good. Then any index I return is the only one. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth elements. Values fit in a normal int.

Here's the thing I want to name up front. Because the array is sorted, I can ask a yes-or-no question at every index: is this value at least the target? The answers look like a run of no's followed by a run of yes's, and they never flip back. So the array has one boundary, and the first yes is the only spot the target can live in. That reframes the job: I'm not hunting for an equal value, I'm finding that boundary, then checking one cell.

Let me run through the example. With minus one, zero, three, five, nine, twelve and target nine, the first yes is at index four, and the value there really is nine, so the answer is four. With target two, the boundary is index two — but that value is three, not two, so I return negative one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would walk the array from the front and compare every value. That's correct, but it's linear and throws away the sorted order, and the problem asks for log n, so that's out. This problem reminds me of a lower-bound binary search — a binary search written as a boundary search. One common style checks for equality inside the loop and returns early. The other only shrinks a range and checks once at the end. I'll take the second one: it has two branches instead of three, and the same skeleton answers any first-position-where-a-condition-turns-true question. One shape, many problems.

Here's the plan. One: keep a half-open range, left to right, starting at zero and n — everything before left is a no, everything from right on is a yes. Two: while the range isn't empty, check the midpoint; if its value is at least the target, set right to mid, otherwise set left to mid plus one. Three: after the loop, left is the boundary — return it if it's in range and holds the target, else negative one. One thing worth flagging — the branches are asymmetric on purpose: a mid that passes could be the boundary, so I keep it; a mid that fails is proven too small, so I drop it. The three-branch version can stop early on lucky inputs, but both are log n in the worst case. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The range starts at zero and n. Inside the loop I take an overflow-safe midpoint, then either pull right down to mid or push left past mid. After the loop, left is the first position whose value is at least the target. One thing worth flagging — the left equals n check is not a speed thing, it's a correctness thing. When every value is smaller than the target, the loop ends with left equal to n. That's a valid past-the-end position, but not a valid index. If I read the value at left first, I'd read off the end of the array. So the order of those two checks matters.

Let's dry-run the code with minus one, zero, three, five, nine, twelve and target nine — expected four. The row that matters is the last: range four to five, mid four, value exactly nine. The test is at-least, so equal is a yes; right drops to four and the range empties. Left is four, not n, and holds nine, so I return four. That matches. Corner cases: target two, missing in the middle, ends on a three, so negative one. Target one hundred ends at n, and the guard fires first. Target negative one, the very first cell, returns zero. A single five with target negative three returns negative one.

The time complexity is log n: each round at least halves the range, so ten to the fourth elements take about fourteen rounds — and a missing target still pays all of them. The space complexity is constant, a few ints and no recursion. Why the loop always ends: with left below right, mid sits inside the range, so both right equals mid and left equals mid plus one shrink it. Writing left equals mid instead could loop forever on a two-cell range. Oh, one more thing — I wrote the midpoint as left plus half the gap. Here it doesn't matter, but over a value range near the int limit, left plus right can overflow — a famous bug even Java's library binary search once had. So I always write the safe form.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed the search as finding a yes-no boundary before writing a line, which is why your loop has two clean branches instead of three. You explained the asymmetry between right equals mid and left equals mid plus one as a termination argument, not a style choice. And you called out the left equals n guard as a correctness requirement with the right check order. Good work.
